An AI coding agent can give a product manager a working prototype before the next planning meeting. Which is great! But someone still has to decide whether any interactions make sense, the new features solve a problem, or — most importantly — whether the team can ship it safely.

At Octopus Deploy, that’s changing how product managers pitch new features. The company is asking them to bring a prototype in place of a written requirements document and keep refining how the feature works, says Dan Garfield, its VP of Open Source. A developer can then take it the rest of the way to production.

“The ultimate differentiator now seems to be care, attention to detail, and taste.”

“The ultimate differentiator now seems to be care, attention to detail, and taste,” Garfield told The New Stack’s Matt Burns at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City. Their conversation moves from talking about a free tool that catches risky Argo CD configurations to a bigger question facing developers who use AI to write code. For example, what happens when the team can produce changes faster than it can verify and deliver them?

A checkup for Argo CD

Garfield, an Argo CD maintainer, recalls a community member whose instance suddenly deleted 100 applications. They recovered quickly, but figuring out what happened took some digging. Two settings that were fine on their own could, together, let a network error trigger the deletions.

That’s the sort of surprise Octo Doctor, a free, open-source tool announced at ArgoCon, is meant to catch. It scans Argo CD configurations against a deterministic rule set drawn from years of maintenance and customer work. Its report explains what a setting could do and how to address it. Developers can run it from the command line, invoke it as a Claude skill, or add it to CI to catch risky pull-request changes.

“It’s a tool that you can run using AI, but it gives you a deterministic output,” Garfield told TNS.

The guidance leaves room for judgment. A team might have good reasons to keep a flagged configuration. The report lets developers weigh that choice with a clearer picture of what could go wrong. Ideally, they get to have that conversation before 100 applications make it for them.

When the bottleneck moves to delivery

In Garfield’s account, more AI-assisted coding puts pressure on source control and then on CI as teams open and revise more pull requests. Once those changes pass CI, developers still need evidence that the software behaves correctly in an environment that resembles production. Octopus Deploy’s continuous delivery platform works with Argo CD and handles steps such as testing, approvals, and promotion from staging to production.

Garfield describes how those steps can work together. A short-lived environment gives a chance somewhere to run its tests. Staging provides another opportunity to validate it. A progressive rollout can expose a change to a small share of users, giving teams a chance to catch trouble and revert before it spreads. Policies can spell out which checks and approvals a production service requires, so developers have a repeatable path to release even as the volume of changes rises.

There’s a parallel in how Garfield thinks about GitOps. When he helped write its principles, the group specified versioned, immutable storage. That leaves room to explore how OCI or a versioned database might handle heavier concurrent use while preserving an auditable history.

“There are things that we’re going to have to continue to evolve to handle the scale and change rate,” Garfield said.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack ’s YouTube channel to hear Garfield explain how Argo maintainers use AI to triage and review pull requests, why he still wants predictable builds, and how one person used Google Sheets to do GitOps. They called it “SheetOps.”
